Juvenile recruitment in the Eastern blue groper (Achoerodus viridis) begins with the emergence of prolarvae following a brief incubation period. At a water temperature of 19 °C [T = 19 °C], hatching occurs approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days] after egg fertilisation, a rapid developmental onset typical of labrid fishes spawning in warm temperate waters. The newly hatched yolk-sac larva measures a mere 0.30 cm [Lb = 0.30 cm] in total length, reflecting the small initial size common among pelagic-spawning teleosts. These yolk-dependent larvae drift in the plankton for several weeks before undergoing the metamorphic transition to benthic juveniles, a phase characterised by considerable mortality. Upon settlement in shallow rocky reef habitats, the growing juveniles begin to exploit a diet of crustaceans and molluscs, initiating a period of rapid somatic expansion. The standard length at which individuals attain puberty has been recorded at 20 cm [Lp = 20 cm], a threshold that marks the onset of gonadogenesis and the transition from the immature to the sub-adult phase. Field surveys consistently indicate that this length is correlated with the development of secondary sexual characteristics and the initial activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis.

As individuals progress toward their adult body size, growth rates gradually decelerate, a pattern common among long-lived fishes. The ultimate standard length attained by fully grown Achoerodus viridis reaches approximately 72 cm [Li = approximately 72 cm], positioning this species among the larger members of the Labridae within its temperate Australian range. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet weight recorded for large, reproductively active adults is about 3600 grams [Wwi = about 3600 grams], a substantial body mass that requires several years of sustained foraging to achieve. Growth trajectory analyses based on otolith increment counts suggest that the asymptotic size is approached slowly, with individuals continuing to add measurable somatic tissue well into their third decade. Sex-specific differences in maximum dimensions have not been rigorously quantified, but anecdotal observations from spearfishing records indicate that females may attain slightly smaller terminal sizes than males, a trend consistent with the protogynous sexual pattern characteristic of this species. The energetic demands of maintaining such a large body mass in a temperate environment are considerable, and metabolic rates scale predictably with size.

Such longevity has direct implications for population resilience, as it buffers against intermittent recruitment failures. The extended reproductive window allows older females to contribute multiple spawning events over their lifetimes, enhancing overall lifetime fecundity.

A pivotal life-history transition in the protogynous Achoerodus viridis is the shift from female to male function, a sex change event that is strongly size-dependent. Field studies conducted in temperate reef systems at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C] indicate that this transformation typically occurs at a standard length of 52.6 cm  and at approximately 18 years of age. Reaching this size threshold is contingent upon attaining a position of social dominance within the local group, as the largest, most dominant female typically undergoes the transition following the removal or death of the resident male. The gonadal restructuring involves the involution of ovarian tissue and the proliferation of testicular tissue, a process mediated by endocrine signals. Post-transition males often occupy the largest territories and are the primary spawners in the harem. The size at sex change is notably higher than the size at puberty, reflecting the protracted period of female reproduction that precedes the terminal male phase.

The reproductive strategy of the Eastern blue groper is characterised by moderate fecundity and precise seasonal timing, with spawning aggregations forming during the austral spring and summer. Reproductive output per spawning event is variable but constrained by female body size; at a water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], an individual female of approximately 1.4 kilograms can release roughly 9590 eggs per day [Ri = roughly 9590 eggs per day] during the peak of the spawning season. This daily rate accumulates over the spawning window to produce a substantial annual fecundity. The wet weight at puberty, a body condition commonly used as a proxy for energetic readiness, has been recorded at 70 grams [Wwp = 70 grams], indicating that individuals must more than double their mass from the pubertal stage to reach the size at which they undergo sex change. Comparative data from related labrids suggest that such a high weight-gain multiplier between maturity and sex change is a trait shared with other protogynous wrasses of similar ecological habits. The energetic investment in gamete production is offset by the extended lifespan and multi-year reproductive window, which together buffer the population against sporadic recruitment episodes.
